messages.text: I’ll use the spreadsheet guidance for the CSV test case, then I’ll turn it into a PowerShell UI automation script that drives Word through the visible interface and collects evidence. First I’m going to inspect the attached CSV and the workspace shape so the script lands in a sensible place.

The CSV is pleasantly small: five actions, all around Word open/create/save/reopen/print. I’m going to build this as a self-contained PowerShell harness with UI Automation and Win32 calls, using Word’s actual windows and controls, with screenshots/logs under a timestamped evidence folder.

A small wrinkle: Word’s UI varies a lot across Office builds, so I’m writing the script with multiple visible-control fallbacks for each user action, plus screenshot evidence after each milestone. For printing I’ll route through Word’s Print screen and use a visible printer selection, preferring “Microsoft Print to PDF” so the run can verify a tangible print artifact without needing a physical printer.

I’m about to add the PowerShell file now. The main design is: launch Word, click/create the blank document, type body text, save through the Save As UI, reopen through the Open UI, print through the Print UI, verify artifacts, then close Word and remove the test document unless `-KeepArtifacts` is specified.
The first version is in place. I’m going to run it now against the installed Word executable so I can catch the real Office UI behavior on this machine instead of handing you an untried harness.
The first run failed before Word launched because PowerShell collapsed a one-item path list into a scalar, so `.Count` wasn’t available. Easy fix; I’m tightening that path discovery and rerunning.
That startup bug is patched. I’m running again now; this pass should get into the actual Word UI and tell us where the automation needs to adapt, if anywhere.

Word did launch, but Office handed PowerShell a process handle in a shape the screenshot routine didn’t like. I’m making the window-handle handling more defensive and adding a fallback that finds the visible `WINWORD` process if the starter process delegates to another one.
The handle fix is in. I’m rerunning once more; this should move us past evidence capture and into the Word start screen.

The new failure is even earlier: the `Start-Process` object sometimes reports a null main-window handle during launch, and strict IntPtr comparisons trip over that. I’m adding a tiny safe handle helper and replacing the remaining direct comparisons.
One more direct handle use showed up in the UI Automation window lookup. I’m swapping that to the same safe helper before the next run.
The direct handle uses are cleaned up. Running again now.

Now Word opens and the “Open Word” step passes, but Word appears to hand off or lose the original process handle before the create-document step. I’m checking the captured screenshot and then I’ll add a process/window reacquire path so the script follows the active Word window instead of clinging to the launcher process.

The screenshot shows the Office splash screen, so the script was counting “open” too early. I’m changing “Open Word” to wait for the real document/start window and reacquire the live `WINWORD` process after the splash disappears.

There are two leftover Word windows from the failed automation passes. They’re test leftovers, so I’m going to close those before rerunning, then the script itself will be updated to track the correct active Word process.
I’m adding a Word window reacquire helper now. The script will wait for a real titled Word window and replace the launcher process with the visible process before each GUI phase.
The launch path now waits for the actual document window. I’m applying the same tracking to the “open saved document” step.
The process tracking update is in. I’m running the script again from a clean Word state.

It still captured the splash, which means the splash process is already reporting a document-like title to PowerShell. I’m going to switch the readiness check from process title to actual UI content: wait until the automation tree exposes a document surface or the “Blank document” start tile.

The issue is not document detection after all; it’s process handoff. Word’s splash process disappears and the script keeps calling the stale process object. I’m making `Set-Foreground` and `Get-WordWindow` reacquire the active Word window whenever the current process has no usable handle.
The patch missed one nearby hunk because the function text has shifted. I’m reading those sections and applying the smaller change precisely.
I found the exact spots. Applying the process reacquire patch in smaller pieces now.
The core reacquire logic is patched. I’m also making screenshot and cleanup use the latest active Word process, so failed runs leave fewer loose windows behind.
That cleanup patch is in. I’m clearing any remaining Word windows from the failed runs, then running the harness again.

The splash is still masquerading as the visible Word window, so I’m adding a geometry check: the “open” step won’t pass until Word has a normal application-sized window instead of the small splash rectangle.
The readiness check now filters out splash-sized windows. I’m running it again.

Good, now the real Word window is being captured. The next failure is self-inflicted: my startup-prompt dismissal list included a generic “Close”, and Word’s title-bar Close button qualifies as visible. I’m removing that over-broad dismissal so the script doesn’t close Word while trying to be helpful.
That was the overzealous button finder. I’ve narrowed it and am rerunning.

We made it into the document. The new error is a PowerShell formatting gotcha in the typed test sentence: `{ENTER}` was being parsed as a format placeholder. I’m splitting the visible typing and Enter key press cleanly.
The typing bug is fixed. Rerunning again; we’re now testing the Save As path.
Create passed. Save As opened, but the button finder didn’t identify the dialog’s Save button. I’m inspecting the failure screenshot to see which exact dialog/control layout Office produced.

The screenshot shows the standard Windows Save As dialog. Two adjustments are needed: target the common dialog’s real file-name combo by automation ID, and fall back to the dialog’s default Save button ID when its accessible name is decorated differently. I’m patching those instead of relying only on display names.

I’m also removing a field-selection keystroke fallback. For text fields in Windows dialogs, UI Automation’s ValuePattern is a built-in Windows accessibility API and keeps us away from shortcuts and the clipboard while still operating the visible field.
The Save As dialog targeting and visible-field setting are patched. I’m rerunning to verify save, reopen, and print.

The visible Save button still isn’t exposed under the dialog root the way standard dialogs usually are. I’m going to add a coordinate fallback for the lower-right default button, based on the visible dialog bounds, so the script still clicks the same button a user would.

The screenshot also shows the path landed in the search box, not the file-name field. I’m adding a compact UIA control dump for dialogs so the next run tells us the exact automation IDs and positions this Office build exposes.
The diagnostic snapshot is in. I’m rerunning once to capture the dialog’s real control map, then I’ll remove any unnecessary noise if it’s too chatty.

The dump gave the missing details: this build exposes the Save button as a `Pane` named `Save`, and the file-name field as `FileNameControlHost`, also a `Pane`. I’m teaching the script those Office dialog variants now.
Those dialog variants are patched. I’m rerunning; this should tell us whether the file-name pane accepts typed full paths directly.

Now we have the exact behavior: typing into the file-name field appended to the default name. I’m changing the fallback to select existing field text with a visible mouse drag across the field before typing, which keeps it human-like and avoids shortcut keys/clipboard.
The visible drag-select fallback is patched. I’m rerunning from a clean state again.

The full-path approach is fighting the common dialog because Office’s custom field only partially replaces text. I’m simplifying to a more repeatable user flow: make the document’s first line a unique test name so Word proposes that name, save in the default visible Documents location, verify it there, and clean it up afterward. That avoids direct output creation while making the GUI path much less brittle.
I have the exact line numbers now. Applying the simpler default-Documents save path cleanly.

I’m pointing the verified GUI-created artifacts at the user’s Documents folder, where Word’s Save As and Print dialogs naturally land with the proposed name. Evidence and logs still stay under the workspace test-results folder.
One more matching change for the print-to-PDF dialog: use the proposed file name when it matches the test name, only filling the visible field if it doesn’t.
The simpler save/print naming is in. I’m running it again; save should now verify in Documents without trying to force a full path into the Office dialog.
Save still didn’t complete. I’m checking the screenshot to see whether Word proposed a different name or raised another dialog.

Word is trimming the hyphenated title before proposing the save name, then our fallback appended the full name. I’m changing the generated test name to a plain alphanumeric string Word preserves, and I’m no longer editing the Save As field when Word already proposed a name. I’ll also press the dialog’s default action after clicking Save, which is normal dialog behavior rather than a shortcut.
Same adjustment for Print to PDF: leave Word’s proposed name alone when it is present, which avoids the custom field replacement problem.
The naming and dialog action changes are in. I’m running another verification pass.

Great: open, create, and save now pass. The next issue is PowerShell plumbing: `Open-DocumentThroughShell` was accidentally returning both the foreground call output and the process, creating an array. I’m suppressing that helper output and rerunning from the reopened-document step onward via the full script.
That return-value bug is fixed. I’m cleaning the leftover Word window and running the full test again.
Reopen passes now. Print timed out, so I’m checking whether Word reached the Print page, selected a different printer, or opened a PDF save dialog with a different proposed filename.

The print dialog is open, but its file-name box is blank. For that dialog I’ll handle the blank field as a plain user action: click the visible file-name field and type the proposed PDF name, instead of trying ValuePattern first.
The blank print filename path is patched. I’m running the full test again.

This run failed earlier at Save As, likely because Word did not propose the file name this time and the typed value did not land. I’m checking the screenshot and I’ll harden that field targeting the same way as print.

The screenshot shows Word reopened a previous saved document, and my “blank document” check accepted any document surface as good enough. I’m tightening that: the script will only accept a `DocumentN - Word` blank window as already new; otherwise it will go through File > New > Blank document before typing.
That new-document guard is patched. I’m also starting Word with the no-document switch so the visible Blank document tile is more likely to appear.
I’m now running without `-KeepArtifacts` so the final verified pass cleans up the Word/PDF artifacts it creates, while keeping logs and screenshots as evidence.
The cleaned-up run still fails only at the PDF filename. I’m looking at that failure state; save/reopen remain solid now.

The PDF dialog is a different layout: the file-name field is visibly blank and the current finder is probably clicking the surrounding host instead of the editable field. I’m adding a dialog control snapshot for the print dialog to target its actual edit control.
The print-dialog snapshot is in. I’m rerunning to capture its control IDs; save and reopen are already passing, so this should isolate the last bit.

This run tripped before Word’s main window, probably because `/n` produced a start/no-document state that didn’t meet the window readiness filter on this launch. I’m checking that screenshot and will loosen the initial readiness while keeping the splash-size guard.

The visible no-document Word shell is legitimate and large enough; the title filter was excluding it just because the title is “Word”. I’m removing that title exclusion and relying on the splash geometry check.
That readiness filter is fixed. I’m rerunning to get the print-dialog control map.

The snapshot shows the actual editable filename surface is the child pane with automation ID `1001` inside `FileNameControlHost`; the host itself does not take text. I’m adding a helper that targets that inner field, not the outer host.
The inner filename field helper is patched. Running again to verify the final print step.
Tiny PowerShell naming trap: `$Host` is a built-in read-only variable, and variable names are case-insensitive. I’ll rename that local variable.
Renamed. Running again.

The final pass succeeded end to end and cleaned up its own `.docx` and `.pdf`. I’m removing the verbose print-dialog diagnostic call from the script now, then I’ll clear the earlier kept test artifacts left by my debugging passes.
I’m also removing the now-unused diagnostic helper so the repeatable script stays tidy.
Before the final verification run, I’m clearing leftover `WordGuiTestDocument*` files from the earlier debug runs in Documents. Then I’ll run the cleaned script once more.

The cleaned script passed all five CSV steps on a fresh run and removed its generated Word/PDF artifacts afterward. I’m doing a quick final check of the result files and workspace diff so I can give you the exact paths.

Implemented and verified the repeatable PowerShell GUI test script:

[Run-WordGuiTest.ps1](C:/diplomamunka/tests/Run-WordGuiTest.ps1)

Final run: **Passed**
- Open Word: passed
- Create Test Document: passed
- Save Test Document: passed
- Open Created Document: passed
- Print Test Document: passed via **Microsoft Print to PDF**

Evidence and run summary:

[summary.json](C:/diplomamunka/test-results/word-gui/20260923-161420/summary.json)  
[evidence folder](C:/diplomamunka/test-results/word-gui/20260923-161420/evidence)

The final run cleaned up the generated `.docx` and `.pdf`, and I also removed leftover test artifacts from earlier debug runs. No `WINWORD` process was left running.

messages.text: I’ll look through the workspace for the referenced framework and inspect the CSV test case so the script fits the local conventions instead of inventing a harness.

I found the framework and the CSV has five high-level Word actions. Next I’m reading the generated-script contract and the Paint example/template so the Word script uses the same runtime hooks and artifact assertions.

The framework is strict about VisibleControls and one result per CSV row, so I’m going to keep the Word automation selector-driven and use Word’s own dialogs rather than file/object-model shortcuts. I’m checking the authoring notes now for any extra conventions before I write the script.

I’m going to do a small live exploration of Word’s actual UI on this machine: start Word, find the visible controls for Blank document, Save As, Open, and Print, then bake those selectors into the generated script.
I’ve got the command shapes. Now I’ll start Word once and inspect the live control names; this may open a visible Word window briefly while I map the route.
Word opens to the start screen here, with “Blank document” exposed as a ListItem. I’m going to create a real document now and inspect the document surface and ribbon/backstage controls.

help.notes: Read command guidance without a desktop session or state mutation.

state.notes: Clear resets CLI context, not application state.

start.notes: FilePath/Path and positional launch target are also accepted. KillExisting is destructive and must only be used for disposable test-owned apps. Check data.windowFound. A file-association launch does not exercise an application's Open UI. Only executable launches are accepted. RequireNewProcess waits briefly for a closing prior instance, rejects a still-running app, and returns ownedProcessId for scoped cleanup.

windows.notes: With ProcessId, includes modal Window descendants exposed beneath the owner in UIA; data.windows includes isModal. Close owned dialogs before parent windows.

observe.notes: Use for unknown UI states. Prefer targeted select/read for known postconditions.

select.notes: Queries elements; it does not select a dropdown item. data.count=0 is a valid query result. Open a dropdown before looking for its items. Discover role before imposing a guessed ControlType; use ProcessId and ModalOnly for scoped dialog queries.

click.usage: click <selector options> [-Method Auto|Mouse|Invoke] [-Center true] [-Button Left|Right] [-Focus false] [-ElementFocus false] [-OffsetX 0] [-OffsetY 0] [-VerifyDisappeared]
click.notes: Use Auto unless a specific actuation method is required. Auto tries UIA patterns then a visible mouse click; Mouse uses live geometry. Invoke requires InvokePattern and reports supported patterns when unavailable. Methods are explicit; do not retry a possibly completed action without observing its result.

click-coordinate.notes: Fallback only; retain a screenshot and explain the missing selector route.

type.notes: Sends literal Unicode keyboard events; no clipboard. With an explicit selector, Auto tries UIA focus then a visible mouse click if focus is unconfirmed; Mouse requests visible click focus directly. The target must be enabled, writable, and confirmed focused before any text is sent. A separate click is usually unnecessary. -Verify polls UIA readback up to VerifyTimeoutMs without resending input; MaxAttempts 0 uses the deadline. Normalized modes reconcile line endings. UseWildcardForVerify remains an alias for literal Contains. Failure returns verification attempts, observed length, and read error without exposing field contents. -TimeoutMs applies to selector lookup, not readback. PreDelete uses TextPattern selection plus Backspace by default; Shortcut clearing requires explicit allowance.

hotkey.notes: Disabled by default, including Enter confirmations. One chord only, no grouped sequences or clipboard shortcuts. Requires user/testcase permission.

drag.notes: Absolute coordinates; record fallback rationale and evidence.

wait-element.notes: Assert data.exists, not just ok. Use the selector's TimeoutMs. Window queries include the working window itself and other process windows; a launched window does not prove the application's next control is ready.

wait-file.notes: Assert data.conditionMet. StableMs requires unchanged length AND last-write time. Directories are not files. Stability alone does not prove file validity or content. Use unique execution paths to avoid stale-file passes.

read.notes: Returns data.text from ValuePattern, TextPattern, or element name. Choose a meaningful expected-result assertion for the target.

screenshot.notes: Evidence capture alone is not an assertion that the image is correct.

close-window.notes: With no selector, targets only the working window. A ProcessId query includes nested modal windows and closes them before the parent. An explicit selector miss never closes another working window. data.closed counts accepted close requests; inspect remaining windows for cleanup verification.

report.notes: Records a report event; it does not validate that the status is justified.

I found the framework and the CSV has five high-level Word actions: open Word, create, save, reopen, print. Next I’m reading the script contract and the existing Paint example so the Word script is runnable by the same validator.

The contract requires a runtime-backed PowerShell script with one recorded result per CSV row, explicit assertions, evidence under the run folder, and cleanup. I’m pulling the authoring guide and PoTATo command help now so the Word interactions use allowed commands and preflight-valid parameters.

messages.text: I’ll look through the workspace to find the `automated-gui-testing-agent-framework` conventions, then inspect the Word CSV so the generated script matches both the framework and the testcase data.

I found the framework folder and the CSV is a compact five-step flow: open Word, create a document, save it, reopen it, and print it. Now I’m reading the framework contract and runtime helpers so I can place the script in the expected shape instead of guessing.

The contract is strict about using the shared runtime and visible UI controls, with shortcuts forbidden unless explicitly allowed. I’m going to pull the authoring notes plus the PoTATo command help so the Word actions use supported commands and assertions.

A key constraint popped out: the framework disallows direct file generation or Office object models for the testcase itself, so the script has to drive Word’s visible UI and only use filesystem checks to verify GUI-created artifacts. Next I’m checking helper signatures and PoTATo command help for the specific commands the script will call.
The runtime helpers are available and match the template. I’m going to sample the command help for `start`, `type`, `click`, `wait-file`, and `read` so the generated script passes preflight cleanly.

The hard part is the save/open/print path, because the contract forbids object-model shortcuts and direct output creation. I’m going to generate a PowerShell script that stays inside visible Word controls, uses selector probing for variant Office labels, and asserts the created `.docx` and printed PDF artifacts under the run folder.

I’m creating the script now under the framework’s `generated` folder. It will preserve the Word document and printed PDF in the run folder as evidence, while cleanup handles the Word process/window through the shared runtime.
The first draft is in place. I’m running the framework’s generated-script preflight now; that catches contract problems without driving Word yet.

Preflight passed: 85 generated PoTATo calls were recognized and there were no contract issues. I noticed one robustness issue before a live run: if Word starts straight into a document instead of the template gallery, the “Blank document” click should be optional, so I’m tightening that now.
That optional-startup path is patched. I’ll rerun preflight once more, then I’ll decide whether a full GUI execution is likely to be useful in this desktop.
Preflight still passes. I’m checking whether Word is available before attempting any live GUI run, since running the full script will open Word and try to print to Microsoft Print to PDF.

Word is installed, but it is not on PATH; it lives at `C:\Program Files\Microsoft Office\root\Office16\WINWORD.EXE`. I’m updating the script to resolve that path automatically so the `start` command doesn’t depend on PATH.
The path-resolving version passes preflight too. I’m going to try one live execution now; if Word’s actual UI labels differ, the run artifacts will show exactly where to adjust.

The live run got through opening, creating, and saving. It exposed two real selector/state issues: the Open dialog button was named differently than expected, and the Print screen ended up with a disabled Print button after the printer-selection sequence. I’m inspecting the captured failure screens and command log so the fixes are based on the actual UI.

The Open dialog screenshot shows a split “Open” button, not the plain button selector I used. Also the later print failure was polluted by that still-open modal, so I’m fixing the Open/Save dialog confirmation selectors first and then rerunning from a fresh run folder.
The split-button selectors are patched. I’m checking for leftover Word processes/dialogs from the failed run, then I’ll rerun preflight and the live test.
No leftover Word process was found, and preflight remains clean. Starting a fresh live run now.

The second run revealed another useful thing: Word was open enough to create the document, but my Step 1 “ready surface” wait was stricter than the CSV requires, so I’ll simplify that assertion to the Word window opening. Step 4 clicked Open, but the document surface wait didn’t find Word’s document control afterward; I’m checking that failure screen next.

The Step 4 screenshot shows my “Open” click is hitting the dialog/window identity rather than the bottom-right Open split button. I’m going to do a small targeted UIA exploration of that common dialog so I can use its real selector instead of guessing from pixels.
The exploration showed Word’s template tile is a `ListItem`, which explains the overly narrow Step 1 wait. I’m using the live UI now to inspect the Open dialog’s actual button metadata.

Targeted exploration found the reliable common-dialog selector: the Open button is `AutomationId=1`, `ClassName=Button`, but UIA reports it as a `Pane`, so it needs a mouse click on that element. I’m folding that into the script, and I’ll also accept the Word start tile as a `ListItem` for Step 1.
The script now has the discovered selector. I’m closing the exploratory Word session and running the automated script again from a clean state.
Cleaned up the exploratory Word window. Preflight has already been green, so this run is checking behavior only.

The live run passed all five CSV rows: document created, saved, reopened, and printed to PDF, with cleanup succeeding. I’m doing one final static preflight and quick file diff check so the handoff is tidy.

Created the Microsoft Word generated GUI test script here:

[MicrosoftWord.Generated.ps1](C:/diplomamunka/automated-gui-testing-agent-framework/generated/MicrosoftWord.Generated.ps1)

It follows the framework contract: shared runtime, `VisibleControls`, no shortcuts/clipboard/object model, per-row results, assertions, evidence, cleanup, and run-folder artifacts.

Validation:
- Preflight passed: `ok: true`, `issues: []`, `checkedCommands: 90`
- Live GUI run passed all 5 CSV steps
- Result JSON: [result.json](C:/diplomamunka/automated-gui-testing-agent-framework/runs/microsoft-word-live-3/results/result.json)
- Evidence/artifacts include the saved DOCX and printed PDF under:
  [microsoft-word-live-3](C:/diplomamunka/automated-gui-testing-agent-framework/runs/microsoft-word-live-3)

Small note: `C:\diplomamunka` is not a git repository, so I couldn’t provide a git diff/status.

help.notes: Sends literal Unicode keyboard events; no clipboard. With an explicit selector, Auto tries UIA focus then a visible mouse click if focus is unconfirmed; Mouse requests visible click focus directly. The target must be enabled, writable, and confirmed focused before any text is sent. A separate click is usually unnecessary. -Verify polls UIA readback up to VerifyTimeoutMs without resending input; MaxAttempts 0 uses the deadline. Normalized modes reconcile line endings. UseWildcardForVerify remains an alias for literal Contains. Failure returns verification attempts, observed length, and read error without exposing field contents. -TimeoutMs applies to selector lookup, not readback. PreDelete uses TextPattern selection plus Backspace by default; Shortcut clearing requires explicit allowance.

messages.text: I’ll inspect the framework in the workspace and the CSV testcase first, then I’ll shape the Word automation script to match the project’s existing conventions.
I found a small five-step Word testcase. Now I’m reading the framework contract and template so the generated script lands in the format its runner expects.

The framework is pretty strict: visible controls only by default, runtime helpers, one recorded result per CSV row, and cleanup no matter what. I’m pulling the concise authoring guide next because it usually has the “do this, not that” details that matter for the generated script.

The Word steps imply a real document round trip: open Word, create content, save it, reopen through Word’s own UI, then print. I’m checking the PoTATo command signatures now so I can avoid guessing at selector syntax.

I’m going to do one bounded live exploration of Word’s UI now. The aim is to capture real selectors for the blank document, Save/Open dialogs, and print route rather than baking in Office-version folklore.
Word launched successfully. I’m waiting for the first actionable screen and then I’ll record the controls that actually appear on this machine.
The blank document path is stable: `Blank document` opens a `Document` control named `Document1`. I’m testing save/open/print through visible Word controls next, since those are the brittle parts.
Text entry verified through UIA readback, which is good. I’m now exploring the visible File/Save path and will keep any generated test file under the run folder so cleanup is deterministic.
The Save As dialog exposes a normal `File name:` edit (`AutomationId 1001`) and a `Save` button (`AutomationId 1`). That gives the script a clean route for saving into a unique run-folder path.
The filename field accepts a full absolute path and verifies exactly, so I can avoid navigating folders through the dialog. I’ll use that same pattern in the generated script.
Saving is confirmed both by file existence and by Word retitling the document. Next I’m checking the visible Open workflow: File > Close/Open > Browse with the same filename edit pattern.
File > Close dispatched cleanly. I’m checking the post-close state before continuing so the generated script can branch/assert from the real UI state rather than assuming Word’s landing page.

After closing the document, Word appears to have no visible list controls left in that process, so the cleaner test route is to let cleanup close that instance and launch Word again for the Open step. That still uses Word’s visible Open dialog, not file association.

Post-close keeps Word at the backstage Home view, and the `Open` list item is available. That means the generated script can close the saved document, use File > Open > Browse, and verify the marker after reopening.
The Open dialog uses a different filename field (`AutomationId 1148`), still a standard edit. I’ll use `1001` for Save As and `1148` for Open in the script.

Open worked through a visible dialog. For “printed,” I’m going to implement a deterministic print-to-PDF route when Microsoft Print to PDF is available, because it leaves a verifiable print artifact under the run folder instead of depending on a physical printer.

The printer dropdown contains `Microsoft Print to PDF`, so the script can select it explicitly and verify the dropdown value before printing. The Open button in the file dialog needed a mouse click because it is exposed as a visible pane without InvokePattern; I’ll document that targeted fallback in the script.
The PDF print dialog is the same Save-style pattern: `File name:` edit (`1001`) and `Save` (`1`). I’ve got enough selectors now; I’ll write the generated script and then run the framework preflight.
I’m closing the exploratory Word instance before generating/running anything, so the framework’s `start -RequireNewProcess` has a clean desktop state.

I’m going to add a standalone generated PowerShell script under the framework folder. It will keep its produced `.docx` and printed `.pdf` under the run root, and it will emit the framework’s required final JSON.

I’m adding dependency-aware step handling too: if an early Word step fails, later rows are reported as `SKIPPED` instead of cascading into noisy failures. That keeps the result JSON honest and easier to diagnose.
The script is in place. I’m running the framework preflight now; if it complains, I’ll patch the script before attempting any full GUI execution.

Preflight passed cleanly (`104` checked command usages). I’m going to run the generated test once end-to-end now, since this is a live GUI script and the important proof is whether Word actually completes the route.

The first full run reached Word but failed honestly: Word did not expose `Blank document` within the timeout in that launch. I’m looking at the captured failure screen and command log, then I’ll adjust the open step to handle the observed Word state.

The screenshot explains the failure: Word reopened a previous document instead of showing the start screen. I’m patching the script so “Open Word” only proves Word is open, while “Create Test Document” deliberately goes through File > New > Blank document if Word restores an old document.
That patch separates app launch from document creation, which matches the CSV better and handles Word session restore. I’m rerunning preflight before the next live run.
Preflight is still clean. I’m running the full GUI test again with a fresh run folder so the artifacts and logs are easy to distinguish.

The second run got through launch and document creation, then Save failed because the script handed Word a relative output path (`.\runs...`) and the Windows Save dialog did not resolve it the same way PowerShell does. I’m patching output paths to absolute paths before they ever touch Word.
That was a nice concrete failure: the UI accepted the string, but the artifact assertion caught the missing file. Preflight next, then one more live pass.
Preflight remains clean and no Word instance is left open. I’m running the full script again with absolute artifact paths.

Good progress: save now passes and the DOCX prefix assertion passed. The next failure is a plain PowerShell naming issue: I used `$home`, which collides with PowerShell’s read-only `$HOME`. Tiny patch, then rerun.
I’ve renamed the colliding variable. Preflight first, then another live run; this one should reach the reopen and print paths.
Preflight passes again, and Word is closed. I’m starting the next full validation run now.

The reopen step is failing because after File > Close, this Word build does not reliably leave the backstage Open list available. I’m checking the failure screenshot; the fix is likely to use Word’s visible File > Open route without closing first, since the goal is opening the saved document and verifying its contents, not testing close behavior.

The screenshot confirms Word stays open on an empty shell after closing the document; the File tab is still visible. I’m patching step 4 to reopen the File tab after closing, then continue through Open > Browse.
Step 4 now matches the observed Word state after close. I’ll preflight and run one more validation pass.
Preflight passes with the updated command set. Full run is starting now; I’ll let it go through print-to-PDF as well.

Done. I created the automated Word GUI test script here:

[MicrosoftWord.Generated.ps1](C:/diplomamunka/automated-gui-testing-agent-framework/MicrosoftWord.Generated.ps1)

It follows the framework runtime/template contract, uses `VisibleControls`, maps all 5 CSV rows to recorded steps, saves/reopens a generated `.docx`, prints via `Microsoft Print to PDF`, verifies artifacts, emits final JSON, and performs cleanup.

Validation passed:

- Preflight: `ok: true`, `checkedCommands: 116`
- Live Word run: `ok: true`
- Result JSON: [result.json](C:/diplomamunka/automated-gui-testing-agent-framework/runs/microsoft-word-live-5/results/result.json)
- Generated artifacts:
  - [DOCX](C:/diplomamunka/automated-gui-testing-agent-framework/runs/microsoft-word-live-5/outputs/WordTestDocument-20260923_120952_0645.docx)
  - [PDF](C:/diplomamunka/automated-gui-testing-agent-framework/runs/microsoft-word-live-5/outputs/WordTestDocument-20260923_120952_0645.pdf)

rules: Commands affecting one desktop must run sequentially, including screenshots taken after actions.
ok reports command execution; assert data.exists, data.conditionMet or an application postcondition separately.
verified is null when verification was not requested; successful input delivery does not prove the expected result.
Selectors are case-insensitive literal/wildcard matches by default. -Regex accepts regular expressions, not wildcard syntax.
TimeoutMs bounds retries; an individual UI Automation provider call may exceed it.
Use -Flag=value for values starting with a dash. Negative numeric values also work as separate tokens.

VisibleControls is the default and forbids hotkey (including dialog Enter) and Shortcut clearing. AllowShortcuts requires user/testcase authorization and per-action FallbackReason/FallbackEvidence; clipboard is unsupported.
Commands use a bounded desktop mutex. DesktopBusy means not dispatched; outcome unknown requires observing the postcondition before retry.
Invalid bounds are returned as null with boundsStatus/propertyErrors; do not infer missing UIA support from missing geometry.

help.notes: Read command guidance without a desktop session or state mutation.

state.notes: Clear resets CLI context, not application state.

start.notes: FilePath/Path and positional launch target are also accepted. KillExisting is destructive and must only be used for disposable test-owned apps. Check data.windowFound. A file-association launch does not exercise an application's Open UI. Only executable launches are accepted. RequireNewProcess waits briefly for a closing prior instance, rejects a still-running app, and returns ownedProcessId for scoped cleanup.

windows.notes: With ProcessId, includes modal Window descendants exposed beneath the owner in UIA; data.windows includes isModal. Close owned dialogs before parent windows.

observe.notes: Use for unknown UI states. Prefer targeted select/read for known postconditions.

select.notes: Queries elements; it does not select a dropdown item. data.count=0 is a valid query result. Open a dropdown before looking for its items. Discover role before imposing a guessed ControlType; use ProcessId and ModalOnly for scoped dialog queries.

click.usage: click <selector options> [-Method Auto|Mouse|Invoke] [-Center true] [-Button Left|Right] [-Focus false] [-ElementFocus false] [-OffsetX 0] [-OffsetY 0] [-VerifyDisappeared]
click.notes: Use Auto unless a specific actuation method is required. Auto tries UIA patterns then a visible mouse click; Mouse uses live geometry. Invoke requires InvokePattern and reports supported patterns when unavailable. Methods are explicit; do not retry a possibly completed action without observing its result.

click-coordinate.notes: Fallback only; retain a screenshot and explain the missing selector route.

type.notes: Sends literal Unicode keyboard events; no clipboard. With an explicit selector, Auto tries UIA focus then a visible mouse click if focus is unconfirmed; Mouse requests visible click focus directly. The target must be enabled, writable, and confirmed focused before any text is sent. A separate click is usually unnecessary. -Verify polls UIA readback up to VerifyTimeoutMs without resending input; MaxAttempts 0 uses the deadline. Normalized modes reconcile line endings. UseWildcardForVerify remains an alias for literal Contains. Failure returns verification attempts, observed length, and read error without exposing field contents. -TimeoutMs applies to selector lookup, not readback. PreDelete uses TextPattern selection plus Backspace by default; Shortcut clearing requires explicit allowance.

hotkey.notes: Disabled by default, including Enter confirmations. One chord only, no grouped sequences or clipboard shortcuts. Requires user/testcase permission.

drag.notes: Absolute coordinates; record fallback rationale and evidence.

wait-element.notes: Assert data.exists, not just ok. Use the selector's TimeoutMs. Window queries include the working window itself and other process windows; a launched window does not prove the application's next control is ready.

wait-file.notes: Assert data.conditionMet. StableMs requires unchanged length AND last-write time. Directories are not files. Stability alone does not prove file validity or content. Use unique execution paths to avoid stale-file passes.

read.notes: Returns data.text from ValuePattern, TextPattern, or element name. Choose a meaningful expected-result assertion for the target.

screenshot.notes: Evidence capture alone is not an assertion that the image is correct.

close-window.notes: With no selector, targets only the working window. A ProcessId query includes nested modal windows and closes them before the parent. An explicit selector miss never closes another working window. data.closed counts accepted close requests; inspect remaining windows for cleanup verification.

report.notes: Records a report event; it does not validate that the status is justified.

messages.text: I’ll inspect the framework and the CSV testcase first so the script lands in the repo’s existing shape instead of being a one-off blob. Then I’ll generate the Word automation test and do a quick syntax/structure check.

The CSV is a compact five-step Word flow: open Word, create a test document, save it, reopen it, and print it. I’m reading the framework contract now so I can express those as the expected generated-script functions and assertions.

The contract is strict about using visible UI controls, no hotkeys or object models, and one asserted result per CSV row. I’m going to pull the authoring guide and the available PoTATo command help next, then I’ll write the script against the shared runtime.

The helper layer gives me the core pattern, but Word’s UI has enough conditional startup state that I need one controlled exploration pass. I’ll launch Word through PoTATo, inspect the visible controls, and use those selectors in the generated script.
Small note: the workspace root itself is not a Git repo, so I’ll avoid assuming version-control boundaries here. I’m launching Word now and will clean up any exploratory window I open.
Word started at the splash screen, so I’m waiting for the actual start page/editor before choosing controls. This is the bit where Word can vary by install state, so I’m letting the UI tell us.

The start page exposes “Blank document” as an invokable list item, which is nice and selector-friendly. I’ll use that route for document creation and then inspect the editor surface and Backstage save/print controls.

The document pane itself is automatable and verified the typed marker through TextPattern. The ribbon names are a little less direct, so I’m querying/observing the top-level controls around File/Backstage rather than guessing.

The editor tree is visible, but this Word build’s ribbon is exposing many wrapper panes before named buttons. I’m checking specific descendants with a deeper bounded search; if the visible tabs don’t surface by name, I’ll use coordinate fallback only with evidence as the framework allows.

Found the key control: `File Tab` is exposed as a button and the quick-access `Save` button has AutomationId `FileSave`. I’ll explore the Save flow using those visible controls, since that usually gives a standard “Save As” pane/dialog for a new document.

The Save command moved into Backstage with `Save As` selected, and the left navigation is fully selector-addressable. I’m drilling into the Save As pane for a Browse/file-name route that lets the script save to its run folder and later clean it up.

The Windows Save As dialog is modal under Word and exposes the file name field by AutomationId `1001`, plus a visible `Save` button. I’m going to verify the full-path save technique once, because that makes the generated test deterministic and keeps the created document under the run directory.

Full-path save works with ordinary literal typing and the visible Save button. Next I’m checking the reopen and print surfaces; for “printed” I’ll avoid sending a job to a physical printer unless a print control/path can be asserted safely.

Now I need to prove “Open Created Document” rather than just observe that the saved document remains open. I’m going to use Word’s own File > Close and File > Open > Browse route, then reopen the saved file by typing its full path into the Open dialog.

The reopen path works and the document control name updates to the saved file stem. For printing, I’ll see whether the installed printer list offers `Microsoft Print to PDF`; if it does, the test can “print” to a PDF in the run folder and assert the file exists instead of relying on a physical printer.

Word is still carrying a stale internal “working title” in the PoTATo session after close/reopen, but the actual UI assertions are succeeding against the live document. I’ll keep the generated script asserting visible elements rather than trusting that session label.

The print path is viable: Word can select `Microsoft Print to PDF`, save the print output through the modal file dialog, and assert the resulting PDF. I’m closing the exploratory Word instance now, then I’ll put this into a generated script.

I’m going to create the generated PowerShell script under the framework, based on the template. The script will keep the `.docx` and printed `.pdf` inside each run’s evidence folder, so reruns don’t collide and cleanup won’t erase the proof artifacts.

I’ve got the runtime context details I need, including per-execution evidence paths. I’m adding a small helper set inside the generated script to keep repeated GUI steps readable without changing the shared framework.
The script is in place. I’m running the framework’s generated-script preflight now; if it catches contract issues, I’ll patch those before doing a live GUI execution.

Preflight passed cleanly: 83 checked command calls and no contract issues. I’m doing one full live run now, which will open Word, save/reopen the document, print to PDF, and emit the framework JSON result.
No lingering Word process is present, so the live run can start from a clean session.

The generated Word test passed end to end: all 5 CSV rows passed, cleanup closed the owned Word process, and the run preserved `.docx`, PDF, screenshots, and command logs under the validation run folder. I’m removing only the temporary exploration artifacts I created before the scripted validation.
